root.name: Indian Defense: Pseudo-Benko
root.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. Nf3 c5 3. d5 b5

overview: Black offers a Benko-style pawn with ...b5 against the d5 advance, hoping for queenside files and pressure on the long diagonal. Most games continue 4.Bg5, ignoring the pawn, after which White develops comfortably and Black needs ...d6 or ...Ne4 to justify the idea. It is a rare sideline compared with the real Benko, which arrives after ...e6 or a different move order.

white_ideas.idea: Decline the pawn with 4.Bg5 and develop naturally
Take on b5 or play e4 to build a centre if Black overextends

black_ideas.idea: Open the a- and b-files against White's queenside
Fianchetto on g7 and pressure the long diagonal and c-file

typical_structures.structure: Benoni-type asymmetry: White pawn on d5, Black c5 and b5 pawns

character.notes: Black is a pawn down for open queenside lines and White has natural development, so play is concrete with both sides taking risks.

gambit.notes: Black plays ...b5 and White can keep the pawn after taking on b5 or ignoring it with 4.Bg5.

soundness.notes: Premature compared with the Benko proper; White can decline and be comfortable, so strong players treat it as dubious.

structure.notes: Fixed asymmetric Benoni-type centre with queenside half-open files for Black.

approach.notes: Seldom chosen by strong players; mainly a surprise against the Benoni move order.

level.notes: Dubious, so not a good first repertoire choice; the ideas are simple but need accurate handling.

sublines_that_differ.name: Benko transposition
sublines_that_differ.how: The real Benko Gambit, with better supported ideas.
